The invisibility cloak uses fractal metamaterials arranged in two layers around a copper cylindrical mirror.
The cloak's outer diameter is approximately 29 inches, enclosing a cloaking region about 24 inches in diameter and 4 feet tall.
The cloak operates over a microwave frequency band from 500 MHz to 1500 MHz, achieving over 50% bandwidth.
Fractal resonators have footprints of 2.3×1.7 cm (inner layer) and 2.7×2 cm (outer layer) with close spacing to enable broadband performance.
The cloak thickness is about 1/6th of a wavelength at the lower frequency edge, making it a thin-skin design.
A human subject approximately 4 feet tall and 15 inches wide was fully volumetrically cloaked inside the device.
Signal attenuation caused by the uncloaked subject was roughly -25 dB compared to the direct path.
With the cloak, the subject's microwave signal was restored to within about 1 dB of the direct path over half the frequency spectrum.
Control tests with a metal cylinder of the same size showed substantial attenuation, confirming the cloak's effect is not due to diffraction alone.
The inner copper cylinder alone blocks the signal and does not produce cloaking.
The two fractal metamaterial layers alone do not produce cloaking; the combination with the copper mirror is essential.
The cloaking effect is attributed to plasmonic transfer involving surface or evanescent waves on fractal resonators.
The cloak design was achieved experimentally without computational optimization due to complexity.
Transformational optics theory has not predicted such large, broadband, high-fidelity cloaks; fractal metamaterials extend practical capabilities.
The cloak's design uses fractal motifs (rectangular Minkowski/Koch iteration two) to achieve low-Q, broadband response.
The cloak was tested using log-periodic fractal antennas and vector network analyzers in an anechoic chamber.
Multipath and ground reflections were minimized to ensure measurement accuracy.
The cloak represents a milestone in diverted imaging capabilities: electrically large, broadband, and high fidelity.
The technology is potentially scalable to infrared and visible wavelengths.
The cloak achieves a 'see-through' effect by diverting microwaves around the cloaked object to the antipodal side.
